items.title: 13.6 Relative thermal stabilities of hydrogen halides in terms of their bond strength

blocks.text: Down the group from fluorine to iodine the thermal stabilities of the hydrogen halides decrease, because the H-X bond dissociation energies decrease (Table 13.5): HF > HCl > HBr > HI. Hydrogen fluoride is the most thermally stable: the high electronegativity and small radius of fluorine give a strong overlap of orbitals and a very strong H-F bond, with the highest bond dissociation energy, 569 kJ mol-1. Hydrogen chloride is less stable than HF but more stable than the others; the larger radius of chlorine makes the H-Cl bond weaker, 431 kJ mol-1. The H-Br bond is weaker still, 366 kJ mol-1, because of the larger radius of bromine and reduced orbital overlap. Hydrogen iodide is the least thermally stable: the very large iodine atom overlaps poorly with hydrogen, giving the weakest bond, 299 kJ mol-1.

blocks.text: Using Tables 13.4 and 13.5, predict which is more exothermic, H2 + Cl2 or H2 + Br2, and explain how thermal stability relates to bond dissociation energy.
